The lateral pain system is spinothalamic tract which crosses over on the same nociceptive entering the medulla. This will result in contralateral (opposite side of body)  deficits.  The medial pain system is the dorsal column medial leminiscus tract which decussates in the Thalamus. This will result in ipsilateral (same side of body) deficits.  The fact that the lesions are in the S1 and S2 cortices means that the patient will have contralateral (opposite side of body) deficits. Therefore the stroke has led to damage of the lateral pain system (spinothalamic tract)  This is why the patient is experiencing less pain on the right side of the body (as the lesions are in the left hemisphere) and struggles to identify the location where they were pinched as this is part of the affective/cognitive side of pain mediation which is carried by the lateral pain system.  In terms of the dorsal column medial leminiscus tract, the fact that the lesions are in the S1 and S2 cortices means that the patient will have contralateral (opposite side of body) proprioceptive deficits. This means the patient will struggle to identify where they are being pinched but it will be on the right side of the body.  The patient is not experiencing a lower perception of pain as the lesions are not in the appropriate areas of the brain for this to occur.

Angiotensin I and II is a key component of the Renin-Angiotensin-System (RAS)The RAS is a hormonal system that regulates the plasma osmolality and blood volume.The rate-limiting step in the RAS is the production of angiotensin I from angiotensinogen by the enzyme renin, which is released by the kidneys in response to decreased blood pressure.Angiotensin I is then converted to angiotensin II by the enzyme ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme), found primarily in the lungs.Angiotensin II is a potent vasoactive substance that causes a rise in arterial blood pressure.It also stimulates the secretion of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex and antidiuretic hormone (ADH) from the posterior pituitary gland.The release of aldosterone and ADH both lead to an increase in sodium and water reabsorption by the kidneys, which increases blood volume and blood pressure.ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which reduces the amount of angiotensin II reaching its receptors.This is the main mechanism by which ACE inhibitors lower blood pressure.ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis, because they prevent the breakdown of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which leads to an increase in angiotensin II.This causes sodium and water retention by the kidneys, and potassium retention.Patients who are on a potassium-sparing diuretic (e.g. spironolactone) should also avoid ACE inhibitors.

The corticospinal tract is divided into lateral and anterior (or ventral) parts. The lateral corticospinal tract synapses on motor neurons that innervate the muscles of the distal parts of the limbs. This allows for voluntary rapid and dexterous movements at individual digits or joints. The anterior corticospinal tract synapses on motor neurons that innervate the muscles of the proximal parts of the limbs. The medial motor pathways control the movements of the proximal axial and girdle muscles. The rubrospinal, vestibulospinal and tectospinal tracts are involved in non-voluntary movements. The rubrospinal tract is involved in non-voluntary movements of the distal muscles of the limbs in response to sensory input. The vestibulospinal tract is involved in non-voluntary movements of axial and proximal limb muscles to maintain balance and posture. The tectospinal tract is involved in non-voluntary movements of head and neck muscles in response to visual and auditory stimuli. Answer is C - inactivation of sodium ion voltage gated channel.  Answer A is incorrect - the sodium potassium pump is responsible for maintaining the resting potential, if this ceased to work then there would be no further action potentials as the membrane potential would be at 0mV. Answer B is incorrect - inactivation of potassium ion voltage gated channel would mean that there is no outward flow of potassium during repolarisation, the cell would fail to repolarise and stay at a high depolarised potential. Answer C is correct - during accommodation there is a slow, prolonged depolarization, this is due to the inactivation of sodium ion voltage gated channels. Answer D is incorrect - activation of potassium voltage gated channel would mean that there is increased outward flow of potassium during repolarisation, the cell would repolarise too quickly and the action potential would be shortened. Answer E is incorrect - activation of Calcium ion voltage gated channel would mean that there is increased inward flow of calcium during the plateau phase of the action potential, the action potential would be prolonged.  Refer to the Case 14 Cardiac action potentials lecture

Type I pneumocytes make up 90% of the alveolar surface and are responsible for gas exchange. They are single-layered squamous epithelial cells.Type II pneumocytes make up 10% of the alveolar surface and are responsible for producing surfactant. They are 6-7 cuboidal cells.Alveolar macrophages are phagocytic cells which engulf pathogens in the alveoli.
